utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we begin, as usual, by taking the appearances, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Good morning, Your Honours. Gramsci Di Fazio, Tom Hannis, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And I believe the usher has gone to get the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. We pick up where we left off on Thursday. And before Mr. Zecevic resumes his cross-examination, I would remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. It's a fact, sir, isn't it, that the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the highest government body in the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On transcript page 12501 from Friday, you were answering the question of my learned friend about courts -- or, rather, it was a question from the Trial Chamber, and the question related to the National Defence Council and Crisis Staffs. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that we spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You stated then, if I understood correctly, that Crisis Staffs were, as you put it, illegal bodies, and that the parties organised them to forward -- or to further party interests.

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. The Crisis Staffs were established by political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that that was completely different from the municipal National Defence Councils which were established pursuant to the Law on National Defence?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were Crisis Staffs in municipalities and in regions as in the SAO Krajina, the SAO Romanija, and SAO this, SAO that. All such bodies were established contrary to the laws and regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina because they were parallel authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that one of the first Crisis Staffs established in Bosnia-Herzegovina was established by the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of BiH?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I have never heard of a Crisis Staff established by the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D108.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is -- these are the minutes of the 35th Session of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of BiH held on 21 September, 1991. You can see the registration number up there. And on the last page, if necessary, I can show you the signature of the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, and of the general secretary of the Presidency, Mile Akmadzic. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us show page 2 to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see item 3 and that is the fifth paragraph from the top. It says: "The Presidency established the Crisis Staff that consisted of Ejub Ganic, Biljana Plavsic, Franjo Borac, the minister of peoples defence, and the minister of the interior, and the commander of the territorial defence, Colonel General Drago Vokosauljevic, and the meeting was held on the premises of the Presidency and the -- it will be -- assisted by ministries and other organs and organisations in the republic.

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it. I said I didn't know that the Presidency established a Crisis Staff. This document shows that it did. But it is also a fact that this Presidency is a multi-ethnic Presidency and the Crisis Staff too, and it consists of representatives of all peoples and all political powers or parties in the Presidency; whereas, the Crisis Staff at municipal level and the Crisis Staffs established by political parties are essentially mono-ethnic Crisis Staffs that were in fact parallel government authorities. Whether this Crisis Staff is a parallel government authority I don't know. I can't comment on that. But the ones I mentioned certainly were mono-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I only showed you this because you said that Crisis Staffs were illegal bodies per se. This is the reason for my showing you this.

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate what you showed me and this is a fact. But can I only reiterate that the Crisis Staffs constituted by political parties at municipal level were certainly parallel government bodies and that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, given the fact that the Presidency constituted a Crisis Staff there must have been a legal foundation for the establishment of such a body. You will agree with me there.

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will not. There was no legal foundation for the establishment of mono-ethnic Crisis Staffs that were -- that were under the influence of political parties and they shouldn't have been established in such a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are insisting on the composition of the Crisis Staffs; whereas, I am insisting on the legal basis for the establishment of such a body. I am not dealing with the question whether or not a Crisis Staff was -- was made up representatives of one people or several peoples and the like. But you will agree with me that the Crisis Staff as a body was provided for by laws and regulations given the fact that the Presidency itself, as early as September 1991, that is, the highest government body in the republic established such a Crisis Staff. I am asking you whether you agree with me or not.

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Speaking about this, it's a fact, isn't it, that at every SJB, including the one headed by you, there was a department for the wartime establishment of the ministry, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no department for the wartime organisation. But there was a department called Department of Defence Preparations. That department engaged in certain activities to facilitate the mobilisation of the reserve police force in crisis situations. They would supply equipment and train personnel for crisis situations but not -- they were not focussed on war and wartime conditions; although, that also could have been one of the objectives of that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that department also organised or took part in the organisation of the MUP or making plans for that in wartime situation or in imminent threat of war, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document 1D034351.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this document is dated the 2nd of October, 1991. It's a coded dispatch which was sent from the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was signed by the Assistant Minister of the interior, Mr. Avdo Hebib. It was sent out to all the CSBs and all SJBs as well as the SUP of Sarajevo, and therefore I assume that you also received this document. It is about the very thing we were speaking about, the Department of Defence Preparations. It says the staffing issues wartime organisation of the police, et cetera. Have you seen this document?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I received it as an SJB chief. I haven't seen it for 19 years. I don't remember the document, really, but I believe that I got it, because I must have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you need minute to review it and to jog your memory and then I will ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours, please, I think you should note there's a -- I believe, a mistake in the English translation. It's probably not important. It says the 3rd of October. It should be the 2nd, from looking at the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you refreshed your memory?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it through.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document relates to what I have just said, the Defence preparations of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It also shows that the MUP monitored the situation with regard to staffing, the wartime organisation of the police in the Socialist Republic of BiH, and it puts forward some views and observations regarding that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Look at the fifth paragraph from the top. It says: "The Sarajevo police stations shall submit one copy of this dispatch containing the above data to the Sarajevo SUP." Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the last paragraph of the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just repeat your first answer? I asked you whether you saw that but you answered too fast. I wasn't able to switch off my microphone.

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. It's the last paragraph on page 1, about police stations in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there's no objection, I seek to tender this document. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection, if Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D336, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 1D034354.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is yet another document of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The date is 31st of January, 1992. It's an open dispatch, not coded, and it was signed by Assistant Minister for Internal Affairs, Mr. Jusuf Pusina. This document too was sent to all CSBs, SJBs, and the Sarajevo SUP. You see that in the heading?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, and it's correct. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember receiving this document?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have received it. I don't remember the specific document and its contents, but based on the position that I held at the time, I had to receive this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Shall I give you a couple of seconds to go over this document to refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's not entirely clear ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the -- this be zoomed in so that the witness can read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was typed up on a typewriter and then the document was photocopied so that's why it's so unclear. But I have understood the gist of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a MUP instruction about abiding by the order for providing information, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Police just like any other established organisation, has its own methodology of how, when, and who communicates with whom and who requests information from whom and so on, and I can see from this document that it addresses the issue of some people not following the established practice and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you. This is how I understood this document too. In addition to that, in paragraph 4, in the last sentence, it says: "MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, insists on receiving full and timely information about all security-related events." Right?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was legal duty of chiefs of all CSBs and SJBs. This is what they had to do under the law. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in this document, the MUP insists that the procedure for providing information be respected, both within specialised lines of work and in the sense of hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the hierarchy, both horizontal and vertical had to be respected, and Mr. Pusina was assistant minister for police affairs, and he must have seen that there were some deficiencies in the system; therefore, he issued this instruction ordering that all deficiencies and faults be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections I tender this document into evidence. MR. DI FAZIO: No objections, if Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D337, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, during your evidence on Friday, you and I disagreed on the status of the secretariat of the interior of Sarajevo. Do you remember that we had opposing views on that?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that we did not agree on all matters, but I don't know what exactly you have in mind now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, my position is that all stations of public security from the territory of the town of Sarajevo were within the Sarajevo SUP and that via the Sarajevo SUP, they came under the Sarajevo CSB.

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have full respect for your position, but it is not correct. And I will repeat it once again. The centre of CSBs, there were 21 stations, and within it, the city stations were not particularly outside of it. And the Sarajevo SUP was part of the organisational structure of the Sarajevo CSB. This is what I said on Friday, and this is what I'm repeating now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court usher assist me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will give you an excerpt from a document, but let me ask you this first. Have you read the rule-book on the internal organisations of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it. I don't know what exactly you have in mind, but I certainly read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is P850.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I gave this to the witness so as to give him the entire text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn to page 5, please, in e-court. Page 5. MR. DI FAZIO: Could I know which Article we're going to deal with? If you to just tell me the number, then I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 6. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the corresponding page in English, if there is an translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: See, sir, in Article 6 of this rule-book on internal organisation it says that: "Exceptionally within the centre of security services of Sarajevo, there shall be a Secretariat of Internal Affairs of Sarajevo for the territory of municipalities which comprise the town of Sarajevo and within which there are public security stations established for the territory of the municipalities which comprise the city of Sarajevo." This means that the municipality where you were the chief and which comprised the group of municipalities within the city of Sarajevo came under the secretariat of the interior for the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the first page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it is a fact, isn't it, that the Law on The Interior Affairs of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at that time, in 1992, still had the term "secretariat" in its text, not the ministry. It was called the republic secretariat not the republic ministry. Regardless of the fact that in common life people frequently addressed it as the ministry. However, the law spoke of the secretariat. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, and I remember that that was the term used by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 16, which is page 19 in e-court, and we need Article 29. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, there's a part of the text that I think needs to be redacted. And that is at line 14 where the witness reveals his -- his occupation and position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree. I'm sorry. It was the witness who -- who mentioned it first and then I -- I -- I -- I repeated. I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, sir. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I missed the actual part in the question as well. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So both parts need to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] See, sir, Article 29 speaks about the Sarajevo CSB, and it establishes the organisational units that the Sarajevo CSB has. And then under 1 it says: "The public security services sector comprises the following organisational units," and then they go on to enumerate those units? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then on the following page, which is page 20 in e-court, we're still within the same Article, Article 29, and here they go on to enumerate other organisational units of the Sarajevo CSB. And under item 2, you see that there is a department for affairs of aliens. And then under 3, we have the department for materiel and financial affairs. And then under 4, we have the secretariat of the interior of Sarajevo. And it says under 4: "Within the secretariat of the interior for Sarajevo there shall be following organisational units." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then under (a) we see the police stations enumerated, the ones that you mentioned in your evidence on Friday. And that under (b) we have the sector for affairs and tasks aimed at preventing and detecting crime. And then under (c), we have department for affairs and tasks relating to passport and travel documents regulations. And then under (d) and further on, they go on to enumerate public security stations. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 21 in e-court, which is the continuation of this Article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So under item 4 of Article 29, we see that they mention the secretariat of the interior of Sarajevo. And then they go on to enumerate all the organisational units of the Sarajevo SUP. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that in this document, but I see it in the one that's in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely why I gave you the photocopy of the document so that can you follow through the entire document as I'm putting my questions to you because the monitor will only show you page by page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: (redacted). But you see the public security station that you were the chief of. And further in this Article, under 5, we see the Breza SJB, under 6 we have Vojnica SJB. Under 7 we have Han Pijesak SJB. And under 8 we have Kazinovik SJB? Sir, based on this document we can see that what I am claiming, that the Sarajevo SJBs, at least according to this document, came under the Sarajevo SUP; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Looking at this document, one would say so, but that's not how it was in practice. It absolutely wasn't. I would like to have the entire document on organisation of the Sarajevo CSB so that we can see what the position of SJBs was within the Sarajevo CSB. You can see that all of this is mentioned as one whole within the Sarajevo CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I have a document here and it's 480 pages long. These are the regulations on the internal organisation of the secretariat of the republic. And I will give it to you for you to read with pleasure, but for reasons of time restraints, I must continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I wonder if, before you move on to something else, if we could just crystallise the points on which you and the witness seem to have different opinions, because it's not quite clear to me. I thought your point was that all the CSBs were subordinated to the Sarajevo CSB. And -- and so that there was sort of only an indirect link between the CSBs in the countryside with the MUP in Sarajevo, because the CSBs outside Sarajevo would have to go through the CSB in Sarajevo in order to get to the MUP. But can you please just make it clear on the points that we have to -- to take note of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I understand, Your Honours. I will gladly do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we must clarify, both of us, matters to the Trial Chamber as best we can. It's a fact that the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BiH consisted of nine Security Services Centres, CSBs, one of which was the CSB of Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As opposed to the other eight CSBs, only the Sarajevo CSB, in its structure, had an organisational unit called the SUP of Sarajevo or secretariat of the interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I say Sarajevo SUP, I mean the secretariat of the interior of Sarajevo, the head of which, at the time, was Mr. Mico Stanisic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Within the CSB of Sarajevo, as well as in all other CSBs, there were organisational units called public security stations or SJBs. But in Sarajevo, apart from SJBs, there was also this organisational unit called the secretariat of the interior of the city of Sarajevo. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The CSB of Sarajevo comprised the territories of 21 municipalities in the Sarajevo region. Every Municipal Assembly had one public security station, SJB. 21 SJBs, the Sarajevo SUP, and the other organisational units from the CSB, including the SUP, made up the CSB of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Where you and I differ is my position that all municipal SJBs from -- from the territory of the city of Sarajevo were part of the SUP of Sarajevo and were linked to the CSB via that SUP. You say that the SUP of the city of Sarajevo was only one organisational unit; whereas, all SJBs, including the ones in the city of Sarajevo, among which there was yours also, are directly linked with the CSB. This is where we have different opinions, right?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completely understand your position, but I can repeat that this was how we functioned in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A minute ago I showed you the rule-book on internal organisation, and you aid greed with me that under this rule-book -- or from this rule-book it follows what I say. Namely, that the SJBs in the city of Sarajevo were subordinate to the SUP of Sarajevo and only through it were they linked to the CSB. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a possible interpretation on what we have read in this rule-book. But we didn't function that way. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I will read to you P510, which is the third page of the Law on Internal Affairs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated 29th of June 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 26. Article 26, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which says -- you can see here, in Article 26, it says the secretariat of the republic rather than the ministry of the republic?

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But essentially it's the same. This mustn't be a contentious matter. It really isn't in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Article 2 -- sorry, paragraph 2 of this article says: "Within the CSB of Sarajevo, the Secretariat of The interior of Sarajevo is also established as an organisational unit of that centre for the territories of the municipalities that make up the city of Sarajevo." This, again, illustrates that my -- that my claim is covered by what the law says.

utterances.speaker: ST-155 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fact that this is what the law says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to move on to a topic that is more directly related to the witness. I suggest that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Since on your last appearance you would have been released as a witness, it is necessary for you to make the solemn declaration again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may be seated. The reason why you are back before us is that there is an application to which the Trial Chamber has acceded, that the Defence be permitted to ask further questions of you in cross-examination. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- to tide the record, Mr. O'Sullivan, would you, sir, please repeat for us your -- yes, I'm -- I'm just interrupting myself to go into private session, bearing in mind the protective measures that have been employed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention, sir, to the 30th of September, 1992 for my first question, okay? On that day, September 30th, 1992, did a funeral take place in Vlasenica for 29 Serb soldiers who were killed on the front lines at Rogosija?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a funeral. You say it was on the 30th of September, so I believe that was the date. I think that 29 members of the VRS were buried who were massacred and killed at the separation line or demarcation line at Rogosija.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you attend that funeral?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: At the time, I was at the funeral, but I also secured the ceremony, because the funeral took place in Vlasenica at the veteran's cemetery. There were other personalities present, so I brought in additional police from other police stations to secure the place because tensions were high.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: While you were at the funeral did you speak with Dragan Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like now to turn to the following day, October 1st, 1992, the day after the funeral. On that day, the following day, after the funeral, did you meet with Dragan Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Because I was busy doing the work of chief. I had other business to attend to. If I transmitted orders, they were police orders, but he wasn't a member of the police so there was no need for me to see him or talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. Excuse me, for my technical problems here. I'd like to move to another topic and ask you whether you were aware whether an operation was conducted in the village of Zaklopaca in mid-May 1992. Were you aware of any such operation?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: I learned about that event only on the following day, after the event. I didn't hear about it from any other sources. There were many people wanting to leave Vlasenica, and there were buses that were taking people to Kladanj. On that day the number of people who wanted to leave had risen and Zaklopaca isn't far from Vlasenica, so I heard that there had been an incident down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Following that operation, this would be mid-May 1992, did Dragan Nikolic have a conversation with you, Miroslav Kraljevic, about the fact that there was agreement that the killings which took place during that operation should be condemned? Did a conversation like that take place?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Well, it's been a long time, but I don't believe that there was such a conversation because I didn't need to speak to him about anything because at the time he was a member of the TO. He belonged to a special unit of sorts, I don't know what exactly it was called, with the TO and later on he became a guard at Susica. I only knew him as a citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now a different topic, or questions about a different topic. At any time in 1992, any time, did you permit members of the reserve police at the SJB Vlasenica to misappropriate non-Serb houses and to loot non-Serb property?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: I can say with certainty that I never permitted that, nor would I have, ever. In fact, I took rigorous measures against such members, exercising the powers I had under the law. And the measures went as far as dismissing them from service or transferring them to the VRS, and against some of them, criminal reports were filed but whether they were followed on later, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question. Did you ever permit members of the special unit that was under the command of Kraljevic to misappropriate non-Serb houses or loot non-Serb property?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: No. I'm saying explicitly, and it was also the position of the ministry at the time, although it was only yet being constituted. The position of the ministry [realtime transcript read in error "minister"] was very clear that attempts to commit crimes must be prevented, and I made an effort to control the situation to the best I could. So nobody, either explicitly ordered, nor permitted such acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this may be a good timed for the break. There is one thing in the transcript. I thought I heard the witness say he said "the position of the ministry" and the record shows "the position of the minister." I believe he said "ministry."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you ask him the question again to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well -- but through interpretation, I heard "ministry."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: 20 minutes. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, can I now direct your attention to the end of May 1992. That would be the 30th or the 31st of May, 1992. Were you aware whether an operation was conducted in the village of Gradina involving the unit led by Miroslav Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I think it was at around that time, late May/early June. A military operation was conducted by the Army of Republika Srpska, or by parts of the former JNA. And it is most likely that that unit also participated in it. At the time, that unit belonged to the Territorial Defence of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On the day of that operation, were you present at a meeting at the SJB building in Vlasenica, a meeting at -- that took part at daybreak, when the details of the Gradina operation were discussed?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what meeting. But, however, during those events and that operation or action, where police partially participated in some form, it is very likely that I was present at that meeting but I'm not sure which meeting have you in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Were you at a meeting attended by Dragan Nikolic, Radenko Stanic, Mr. Kraljevic, Elvis Djuric, and Zoran Stupar?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that those people attended the meeting. Dragan Nikolic did not have such a position as to be present at some official meeting where there were representatives of the MUP or the army or the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions about the Susica camp. And I am -- I'll direct your attention to mid-June 1992. In mid-June 1992, did Dragan Nikolic report to you and Miroslav Kraljevic about the security situation at Susica? Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Once again, Dragan Nikolic could not inform me directly. There was simply no basis for that. Neither he was a member of the MUP nor was he eligible to inform me on anything on the basis of the subordination. Therefore, he never informed me or reported to me on anything. I don't remember talking to him about any security-related situations of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I've heard your answer, but I'll ask you the following question and you can tell me whether confirm or deny it. Did you receive reports from Dragan Nikolic by telephone regarding the security situation at Susica?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: No. I did not receive any sort of reports from Dragan Nikolic because he was not subordinated to me. If we needed any sort of report from Dragan Nikolic, then it went via Territorial Defence, or, later, via the Army of Republika Srpska once it was established [realtime transcript read in error "sustained"]. Those were the line of communication between us; me as chief of the SJB and them. And as for me receiving reports from individuals such as Dragan Nikolic directly, my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I just have one question about that's recorded in the transcript at line 22. The word us "sustained." I thought I heard the witness say "established." It's not a great difference, but perhaps that could be checked after court.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, here is my next question for you. Did you ever issue orders or authorise the release of anyone from detention at Susica to undergo interrogation?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Did you -- oh.

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Given that there were commissions within municipalities and various relevant institutions, there were commissions for exchange, commissions for communication with ICRC. We, as the ministry, could not issue an order to have somebody released, exchanged, or anything else done with them. We simply were not authorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I've heard your answer, but I'll ask you two more questions which you can either confirm or deny. Did you ever issue orders or authorise the release of anyone detained at Susica for exchange or transfer?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: No. That was within the jurisdiction of the competent commission. Commission for Exchange, I think, existed within the municipality, within the municipal organ. In addition to that, they also had an organ that communicated with the ICRC and that's how it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And did you ever issue orders or authorise the use of a person detained at Susica for work duty?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: No. No, as I have said, that was within the competence of municipal organs who occasionally engaged them for certain works. Given that there was a warehouse of the ICRC in that region, some of them went to work there, and later on, I saw them performing some work within communities, within communal services. But that all existed within a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Between June and September 1992, did you ever visit the Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: No. I said so last time. I never went there for principle reasons, but also because it wasn't within the competency of the ministry. And I also had some principles of mine that prevented me from going there.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Did Dragan Nikolic ever report to you in person at the SJB building concerning Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I explained already how chief of communications went to see the chief of the station to discuss security-related matters. It is possible that he informed somebody at a lower level, but he never talked to me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about early July 1992. In early July, did you learn whether a man named Ismet Dedic had died at Susica?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In the same -- in the same period, did you learn whether a man named Mevludin Hatunic died at Susica?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Between mid-June and the end of September 1992, were you ever present at any meetings of the Vlasenica Crisis Staff when Dragan Nikolic reported to the Crisis Staff on the security situation at Susica?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: I never went to any Crisis Staff meetings because I was not a member of the Crisis Staff. However, the situation with the Crisis Staff in Vlasenica was quite peculiar, because that Crisis Staff never really started working. Rather, it completely stopped working sometime in June, when the commission of the president of the republic was established. Therefore, I can't remember anything regarding those meetings, and I don't think that Dragan Nikolic ever informed anybody at that level. Dragan Nikolic was a guard, a member of the TO. I knew him as a private citizen. And all his [as interpreted] channels of communication followed the institutional ones: Chief of the station, chief of the army, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, just to be sure, the response that you just gave to counsel, did that include also meetings in the War Commissions that were established subsequently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure which commissions you have in mind. But if we're speaking of the Dragan Nikolic, I can assure you that I never attended any official meetings where he was in attendance as well. He simply wasn't the person competent enough to give relevant information, relevant report on security-related matters or any other issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But I suppose the point that counsel is making is that Mr. Nikolic was, after all, the warden of the Susica camp, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, listen, if we have enough time I would like to clarify briefly. Later on, in the trial against Nikolic, it was established that he was the warden of the Susica camp which wasn't true. He was a guard there, or the leader of the shift. This is what I learned later, after I did my research. Namely, that quite a different person was the warden or whatever the title given by the Crisis Staff was. Later on, after analysing the facts I established that he actually never served as a warden. Rather, he was guard or the shift leader or something of that nature, depending on how that part of the service was organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I better give the floor back to Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Perhaps one more small question, Mr. Witness. Do you know the name of the warden then? The name of the person you think was the warden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, later, after analysing and after these trials started, it was established that Veljko Vlasic [as interpreted] had the appointment letter issued by the Crisis Staff or some other competent body at the time. This was proven later on in various investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one intervention in transcript, 56, 13. It is recorded here: "And all his channels of communication followed the institutional ones." I believe the witness said "all my channels," because from the context of his answer it can be understood as -- as this is -- this is referring to Dragan Nikolic where, in fact, he was referring to himself. Maybe this can be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, could you please clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I didn't express myself clearly. But all lines of communication were institutional, all my lines of communication. I only communicated with institutions. I communicated with the chief, with president of the municipality, commander of the army and so on, which is to say that Dragan Nikolic could not participate in any significant matter -- manner at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more question about the transcript. In answering the Judges question you named the person that you thought was the warden. You said his name was Veljko. Could you repeat his last name, please, with a B.

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Basic, B-a-s-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Was -- did counsel for Zupljanin join in this application for further cross-examination? Can you remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We don't have questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, anything arising?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness 179, my name is Tom Hannis; I'm a Prosecutor. We have never met before. I'm standing in for Mr. Olmsted who you previously dealt with when you testified earlier. I want to ask you, first of all, if I can find it, at page 49 today, Mr. O'Sullivan asked you about the funeral that took place in Vlasenica at the end of September 1992. And mentioned that tensions were high, and that's why apparently you brought in extra security. What precisely were the tensions about? What were you concerned about that caused you to bring in extra police?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I did not complete that thought at the time. Since 29 local young men from Vlasenica were killed, there were tensions there among families, relatives, and friends of those who were killed. Also, defence line at the time was weakened because many people had left the positions and so on. This is why I asked for reinforcements in police forces from neighbouring stations so that we could properly provide security during that gathering in view of the existing tensions. And also, should there be any attacks on the demarcation line, so as to prevent any further escalation that. That was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it also one of your concerns that there might be some sort of retaliation against non-Serbs who still remained in Vlasenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Among other things, yes, so as to control tensions of any sort as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did that concern about non-Serbs also extend to non-Serbs who were detained in Susica camp, at the end of September?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Whatever fell within the competency of the police, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. O'Sullivan whether you spoke to Dragan Nikolic at the funeral, and you said no. My question was: After the funeral, did you have occasion to walk with Minister Ostojic, the minister of information? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Whether I walked with him, I don't think I walked with him. But since there were well-known persons at the funeral from the level of the republic ministry, I provided security, and it is possible that I was there at the location where they arrived and that I greeted them or did something of that sort. But my main task was to provide security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall accompanying him or any of the other high-ranking visitors after the funeral? Walking away from the place where the speeches were made, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Well, let me try to remember. The president, Mr. Karadzic was present at the funeral. I didn't have an opportunity to speak to him. We only received him at the stadium. I believe that he was flown in by helicopter and then we escorted him to the funeral site. And of the ministers, possibly there was Velibor Ostojic. I may have spoken with him. But I don't remember any other persons who may have been there, but certainly it was a high-risk gathering as we call it from the security point of view, and we had to take adequate measures to provide security for the reasons I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you not remember anyone speaking --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this. I don't know how this additional questioning arises out of my specific question on cross-examination on whether or not the witness and Mr. Nikolic had a conversation at that time. We've gone quite far afield, I think, of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can respond but I probably should do it out of the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- you do intend to respond to the objection, do you, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you're inclined to grant it, I do intend to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we need to hear you, so in that case, if the witness could be escorted from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do you know whether the witness understands English, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know. I have not dealt with him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Given what's been said, I think the redaction has to start page 61, line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: This witness, having been brought back, admittedly for a specific purpose, the issues now raised by Mr. Hannis, whereas, as I indicated earlier, are outside of the carefully drawn cross-examination pursued by Mr. O'Sullivan, nevertheless appear to be relevant and important, and I'm going to allow the question to -- the -- the question be put to the witness. But inasmuch as it is -- goes outside of the -- Mr. O'Sullivan's intent, we'll have a -- we -- we would allow him to -- to re -- cross-examine, further cross-examine the witness on that particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] So you may escort the witness back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry for that, Witness. The question I started to ask was whether on the day of the funeral, do you remember anyone raising the issue or the concern with you about the non-Serbs detained at Susica camp and whether there might be some retaliation out there.

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: I don't remember any meeting about that. As I said, I was in charge of security. If there was a meeting at another level, then there may have been one at the political level, but I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You said at page 49, line 20 today, that Dragan Nikolic wasn't a member of the police so there was no need for you to talk -- to see or talk to him. When did Dragan Nikolic stop being a member of the police in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: He has actually never been a member of the police. And here's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no. That's okay. Let me follow up, and then maybe you can explain. I want to show you an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's my understanding this document is under seal, Your Honours, so if we cannot broadcast it. I'd like to look at page 3. No, I'm sorry, page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, my English translation of this document says that at the top of the page this is a list of members of the special platoon at the Vlasenica SJB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And number 1, Miroslav Kraljevic. It's my understanding that he was the commander of that special platoon?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see number 23 on the list? That's Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page, just so you can see the stamp and signature, that's your -- your name and your signature, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that's one. I want to show you another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit P1045.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this appears to be a list, Vlasenica SJB, list of reserve workers. Who have worked at this police station in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again, this is another document under seal. If we could not broadcast it, I'm sorry. If we could go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look at that. Again, your signature?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And number 90 -- number 97 is Dragan Nikolic. How about number 92, Goran Tesic. Is he also a member of the reserve police in September 1992 in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: I don't know. You can believe me that there are so many names here ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you wouldn't be signing an authorisation to pay people who were not members of the police, would you?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, just to be sure what does this list exactly show? Because, on the title, as far as can I see, it's a list of reserve workers or workers who have worked at this police station in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So are we just talking about members of the police or people who have done work at the place or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Our position, Your Honour, is that these are reserve police who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could we please clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what these people were they cleaning ladies, secretaries? Something other than reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: The police had its active members and its reserve members, both before and at this time. This is a list of reserve police members, because we were at war, or there was an imminent threat of war so that all members who were conscripts had to be used somewhere. One of the way of using them was to include them in the reserve police forces. Another way was to send them to the VRS. So this is a list of the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Hannis. It was just to be sure so that no doubt is left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask one more question that may help in that regard. I see the persons named at item 94, 95, and 96, there's an indication that they only worked 15 days out of the month and it looks like they only got half the pay. Am I reading that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: That's possible. Indeed, this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 50, line 6, Mr. O'Sullivan asked you about the village of Zaklopaca and events there in mid-May of 1992. You said you learned about that event only on the following day. Do you recall who told you about it.

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: I can't remember who exactly told me, but I received information about there having been an incident at that place by the name of Zaklopaca in the Milici municipality. Possibly my colleague, the chief at Milici at the time, let me know. I cannot be sure, but possibly he informed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 50, line 25, you were asked about whether you permitted any members of the reserve police to misappropriate non-Serb houses or loot non-Serb property. You said you never permitted that. And you said: In fact, you took rigorous measures against such member. Can you give us any details about that, about any of the personnel whom you took action against for that kind of conduct? How many; who; what measures you took.

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes. During that time-period, we tried to take measures to the extent that we were able to given the wartime conditions. One of the sanctions for those who were police members was to dismiss them from service and transfer them to the VRS. There are documents to corroborate that, and during my previous testimony I showed that I dismissed certain persons because of their actions, and one of the things they did was looting and breaking into other peoples' homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At [Microphone not activated] -- I'm sorry. At page 52, line 24 today, Mr. O'Sullivan asked you if you were at a meeting attended by Dragan Nikolic, Radenko Stanic, Mr. Kraljevic, Elvis Djuric, and Zoran Stupar. You said in your answer Dragan Nikolic did not have such a position as to be present at some official meeting where there were representatives of the MUP or the army or the like. I'm -- I don't understand what position would Dragan Nikolic have to have to be at a meeting with you, Mr. Stanic, Mr. Kraljevic, Elvis Djuric, who we saw was also on the list of reserve workers at the MUP, and Zoran Stupar. What position would he have to have to be at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: I have already stated several times that Dragan Nikolic was a guard. Given the hierarchy of any one institution, he was not relevant to be at meetings at any level, be it a meeting of the chiefs or a meeting of the MUP of the municipality or the army, or anything. So I have never been at a meeting where Dragan Nikolic could pass on information or give his view on a certain situation, because he didn't have a position of authority. He didn't -- he -- didn't have the authority to command anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What position did Elvis Djuric have that put him at a higher level than Dragan Nikolic to be at such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Careful, because what probably Dragan Nikolic stated that he was somewhere and Elvis Djuric too with me or someone else. That's very doubtful, because I don't really remember any such meeting where they could be present and discussed things and take part in anything. So I cannot accept that as relevant. Whoever stated that maybe wanted too overstate his own importance; for what reason, I don't know and I can't go into that. But there haven't been any official meetings that he attended nor was he able to deal with such things. He was a guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, no one said in the question that this was an official meeting. Is there some reason that a reserve policeman cannot meet with you as chief of the police about all kinds of police matters?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Well, they could, but I don't see why I should have discussed any sort of strategy with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. At page 53, line 9, in an answer about whether Dragan Nikolic reported to you, you said that he was neither a member of the MUP nor was he able -- or was he eligible to inform me on anything. And I think you went to say that he was a member of the TO. When did the TO cease to exist in the Republika Srpska? Wasn't it after the VRS came into existence?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we've seen evidence -- I think the VRS was created around mid-may and the JNA had left by May 20th or 21st. So what happened to those people who had been in the TO? Didn't they either go to the army or to the police?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the decision of the Presidency or, I don't know, maybe the president, the VRS was established and automatically the members of the TO became members of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 55, line 8, you were asked about whether you ever visited Susica camp between June and September 1992, and you said no, you never went there for principle reasons. Let me show you, first of all, Exhibit P1074. Witness, this is a document that appears to be signed by you, dated the 1st of September, 1992, and it's to the CSB. Again, this one is confidential under seal so could we not broadcast it. And you're reporting about a holding centre in Vlasenica municipality. Is this report about Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if -- if I understand correctly how -- if you didn't visit Susica camp, where did you get the information that you put in this report to the CSB?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Well, you know how institutions communicate with each other. The service in charge of the camp, we requested -- or from them we requested information -- information, which we then forwarded to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How far was the camp from your SJB in Vlasenica? Approximately how many kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Possibly 2 and a half to 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've said you never went there for principle reasons or reasons of principles.

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What were your principles that prevented you from going that camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Perhaps this is not the best occasion, but I'll tell you, I was born and I come from the region where, during World War II, all residents had been taken to the Jasenovac camp. Villages, families were destroyed, and I am an offspring of one such family. So I have this kind of position vis-a-vis the camps. That was my principled reason why I refused to go there. I did not support the establishment of that camp at the time. I said during my last evidence that I fought to the best of my abilities using all means at my disposal to have that conclude and resolved as quickly as possible and in as fair a way as possible, for the entire region.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you're not saying the camp at Susica was like the World War II camp you're talking about, are you?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: No. It's just that the concept of a camp, the way I perceive it, in my head, is a catastrophe. This is the position I had ever since my childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And recording the question at page 56, line 5, you were asked about Crisis Staff meetings. Is it -- am I correct to say you never attended any?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: No. Given that I was not a member of the Crisis Staff. I have already said that the Crisis Staff in Vlasenica sort of did not really exist. In June the commission of the president of the republic was established, and this is when I started attending meetings as a representative of president of the municipality. And prior to that, I never attended the meetings of the Crisis Staff, because I did not hold a position within the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After you became chief of police, did you attend any meetings of either the Crisis Staff or the body that succeeded it, whether it was called a War Presidency or a War Commission? Did you attend any of those meetings in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: All meetings that were held at the level of the institution where I thought that I, as a member of the Ministry of Interior, needed to be present, yes, I attended them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you not recall Dragan Nikolic attending any of those meetings to report about the situation at Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: No. Dragan Nikolic was a guard, a shift leader. He could not attend such meetings. He could convey his report or information to one of his superiors for that superior to report at such a meeting. But Dragan Nikolic never attended such meetings because he was a simple guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you don't know about whether or not he attended any meetings that you were not present at.

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Well, I can't know. But he was not a type of a person who could competently inform some gathering at a certain level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Because there are procedures. There is subordination within the work of institutions. It was like that before the war and it is like that now. There's hierarchy, there is subordination. We have a guard, a shift leader, commander, and then all the way up to, say, general. So Dragan Nikolic could have informed only his immediate superior and then that person could have informed the others, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, who was his immediate superior vis-a-vis Susica camp? Was that Mr. Basic?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: I don't know. But I suppose so, if he was the warden. I don't know whether there was a -- anybody in between them. But his ultimate superior, yes, it was that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Basic ever inform at those meetings you attended about the conditions or situation at Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: No. They belonged to the Territorial Defence. And if they reported to anyone, then, initially, those reports were sent to the Crisis Staff or similar institution. They did not report to the ministry or the SJB, because they were not duty-bound to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. But my question was, did Mr. Basic report at any -- any of those, either Crisis Staff, War Presidency, or War Commission meetings, about the situation at Susica camp because we know the TO was no longer in existence after late May. So it wouldn't have been reporting to the TO.

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: Yes. But the competent municipal organ which took over the duties of the Territorial Defence could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one rather observation, Your Honours. On page 65, line 6, my learned friend asked when Nikolic stopped being member of police in 1992. The witness said he was actually never been a member of the police and here's why, and then he was cut short by Mr. Hannis, and Mr. Hannis says let me follow up and then maybe you can explain. And we were -- the explanation never came. I don't know if that interests my learned friend or it interests the Trial Chamber, but that is the observation that I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I maintain that he was not a member of police, and this is why: He was a member of a special unit within the Territorial Defence. The moment the Army of Republika Srpska was established, which was in mid-May, all members of the Territorial Defence had to become members of the Army of Republika Srpska or another legitimate institution was the Ministry of the Interior. They could have become members of the MUP. Whenever a member of that special unit within the Territorial Defence did not wish to join the Army of Republika Srpska, a political decision was made outside of the Ministry of the Interior that such units would be attached to SJBs. This was done without consulting SJBs and we were not happy with it, and we informed the ministry about it. Later on, the minister issued an order whereby all such political units were removed from the Ministry of the Interior. Dragan Nikolic started out immediately as a guard at Susica, or as something else. And he never performed, nor was he ever under the command of the SJB. There are many people called Dragan Nikolic. It's a very common name and last name. So how come he appears on that list? At that time for somebody to receive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, there's something I think that needs to be redacted from the witness's answer. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, in order for somebody to be paid out a kind of a compensation, that person had to be either a member of the army or a member of the MUP. There was no third option to pay out this so-called salary, which was really nothing, given the inflation. So if that is the person, Dragan Nikolic mentioned in this list, it's possible that he was carried over automatically, by automatous, in order to be paid out some sort of a compensation because he was neither a member of the army nor a member of the MUP, but he needed to be paid out some sort of a compensation, so this was the factual situation. He was a member of the Territorial Defence or, rather, the body that succeeded the Territorial Defence and he performed security in the Susica region. Another matter that I remember now that we're talking about Dragan Nikolic is this: When the security of the so-called camp Susica or the holding centre stopped functioning, I remember seeing him as a member of the military police either within the corps or within the brigade, I'm not sure. That is the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The answer gives rise to one question from me, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If that's the case, sir, why would you sign the pay sheet for people who were not working for MUP as chief of station?

utterances.speaker: ST-179 [Re-called]
utterances.text: I said if this is that person. Nikolic is a very frequent last name, and I couldn't know hundreds of them. So the only reason was for the person to receive a compensation he needed to be either a member of the army or a member of the MUP, but I cannot state with certainty whether this is, indeed, the Dragan Nikolic. I don't know. There are many Nikolics mentioned on that list alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan, did you wish to avail yourself of the right to cross-examine on that point, on controversy between yourself and Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, sir, we thank you for your return to the Tribunal, and now again it is time for me to release you, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when he is gone, Your Honour, may I take the remaining two minutes to address some procedural and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to ask you about the latest communication that I would have seen emanating from your office indicating that have you some witnesses difficulties. Where are we --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour. First of all, though, could I do something covering the previous witness, ST-155. I believe Mr. Di Fazio wanted to tendered the 92 ter package but failed to do so. Those are 65 ter numbers 10391.01 through .12, and 1067.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regarding scheduling.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. This will be Exhibit P1500.1 through 1500.14, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry. Regarding scheduling, we originally had intended to start this witness with ST-137. You will have seen, I think, from the communications that he had some surgery recently. We were told that he is supposed to see a doctor today, and we we're going to get a report about whether or not he is going to be able to travel. I don't have information yet. I don't know how soon we'll receive it. Frankly, I have some doubts that given the logistics for travel for this particular witness that we'll be able to get him before the end of the week, even if he is medically passed to travel. We also had scheduled for this week ST-215. I think you will have seen from the communications that Victim and Witness was not able to arrange all the necessary paperwork in connection with his travel, and he won't be here in time to testify this week. Lastly, regarding scheduling, in connection with ST-137, there's still a pending matter for you to resolve regarding his 92 ter status and whether the amalgamated statement is going to be permitted to be used as the 92 ter and how much time we'll have for examination. And the last one is Ewa Tabeau, the expert who is scheduled to testify before the break, possibly, and I think there is a matter pending regarding her report or her position as an expert. That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we rise today to resume when?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we get information by the end of the day we could convey it to you. Best case scenario is I don't think he could be here before Thursday. So either we have no witness for the rest of week or we might have ST-137 late in the week, Thursday at the earliest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But the position is that there is nobody for tomorrow or Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. We've tried to bring some other people forward or move some around and have not been able to do so. And some that are scheduled in August, I think in fairness to the Defence, if we tried to call one of those big witnesses now they would have a legitimate complaint that they haven't had sufficient notice to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the adjournment provisionally to -- I think we're scheduled to begin -- to sit on the afternoon on Thursday. In this courtroom at 2.15 on Thursday afternoon; but, of course, persons should be alert to being notified in the usual manner as to whether that fixture has to be cancelled. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of July, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
